newsitem.title: PANAMA: INTERVIEW-Panama Canal prepares for 21st century.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Panama Canal prepares for 21st century.

text.p: The Panama Canal's competitiveness as a leading shipping route will be ensured in the 21st century, thanks to an overhaul well under way, the administrator of the world's busiest waterway said.

The widening of the canal and upgrade of the tracking system of transiting vessels and of the railway along it will all provide for better service, Panama Canal Commission (PCC) administrator Alberto Aleman Zubieta said in an interview.

Widening of the Gaillard Cut, the narrowest point in the 52- mile (83 km) transoceanic waterway, will allow 24-hour two-way passage of the large 100-foot (31-meter) Panamax ships. It is expected to be completed by 2002.
"We're putting $1 billion in capital investment into the canal, which will give it 20 percent more operating capacity," as transit is expected to rise steadily, Aleman said.

The most ambitious project, he said, would be to eventually install a third set of locks, adding a lane to the Miraflores, Pedro Miguel and Gatun locks. Shipping agents say it could require over $10 billion in capital investment.
The PCC plans to present the project to shipping clients at the Universal Canal Congress, in Panama City from September 7-10.

Aleman dismissed reports of the possible construction of "dry canals" -- land routes linking the Atlantic and Pacific oceans through Mexico, Nicaragua or Colombia. They would be costly and the Panama canal presents better services, he said. "Having a rail route right next to the canal makes it the best route".
Plans to privatize that railway linking ports at both ends should lead to a complete overhaul. The Panamanian government is in talks with the Kansas City Southern Industries Inc.

"We provide a service to the shipping community and by enhancing this route shippers will have other reasons to choose this place because there will be alternative facilities to move their cargo, making them more efficient," Aleman said.

Safety is also being upgraded. A $29.5 million vessel tracking system will be installed in four stages by 2001. The Enhanced Vessel Tracking Management System (EVTMS) will allow simultaneous tracking of the movements of each ship in the canal.
The PCC also plans to set up a database, to share information with other ports, coast guards and shipping companies.
"We will know if there is any defect in a ship," Aleman said. "We won't compromise on safety."

Panama will take over control of the canal on Dec. 31, 1999, in accordance with treaties signed with the United States 20 years ago. The PCC will be replaced by an independent Panamanian- run body, the Panama Canal Authority (PCA).
Asked about some concerns in the shipping industry on how efficiently Panama will run the canal, Aleman said the Panamanian constitution required it to be profitable.
"It will be financially independent, management will be independent and it will be run like a corporation," he said.
